newsitem.title: UK: Safeway N.Irish shopping trip seen unlikely.
newsitem.headline: Safeway N.Irish shopping trip seen unlikely.

text.p: Britain's Safeway Plc was unlikely to be shopping for an acquisition in Northern Ireland, despite reports that it had its eye on Irish supermarket chain Wellworth, analysts said on Wednesday.
Food retail analysts were sceptical about Irish newspaper reports that Safeway was considering buying the chain, currently part of industrial holding company Fitzwilton Plc .
However, they stopped short of fully discounting such a move, which would mark the British supermarket giant's entry into Northern Ireland.
"There are food retail sales to be had up there, and there are some pretty weak local competitors. So you wouldn't rule it out," said one analyst who declined to be named.
"But there is a danger of oversaturation in such a small market, as well as political uncertainties," he added.
Safeway declined to comment on the reports.

"In a competitive market such as supermarketing there are constant rumours ... Safeway would like to stress that it never comments on market speculation, and that is the position at the moment," a Safeway spokeswoman said.
Safeway's shares rose 3.0p to 382.5 by 1300 GMT.
Wellworth has 39 stores, two of which are in the Republic of Ireland.

One analyst said Safeway would probably have to pay 150 to 200 million pounds ($240 to $320.7 million) to buy Wellworth from Fitzwilton, but he argued that the chain should find other uses for its money.
"Forget about diversification and overseas expansion. Safeway should be giving the money back to shareholders. That's what all good retailers should be doing," he said.
Wellworth's parent, Fitzwilton, is about 15 percent owned by the family of H.J. Heinz Co chief Tony O'Reilly, who is perceived as a shrewd negotiator.
Analysts said they did not see a compelling reason for Safeway to enter Northern Ireland, noting that two of the chain's competitors already had expansion plans there.
British supermarket chain J. Sainsbury Plc opened its first Northern Irish store in Ballymena, County Antrim, in December, while Tesco Plc opened a store in central Belfast the previous month.

"Sainsburys and Tesco have opened the odd store, but the danger is that they'll all rush in, open a lot of stores and pay a lot for acquisitions, and the market will become just as saturated as the rest of the UK," an analyst said.
"You've got all the problems of servicing Northern Ireland from the rest of the UK, and you've got the political uncertainty there," he added. "It's not a very good market."
